Editor.problem: Each number comes from one run per policy. reproduce.sh runs naive once and fix.sh runs budget once. Full jitter is random by design, so a single budget run cannot separate a real difference from noise. That applies to failed orders, seconds to recover and calls per order alike.
Editor.fix: Run each policy at least 3 times. Alternate the order (naive, budget, naive, budget, ...) with fresh pods each time, and use a separate order-number range per run. Report each run plus the median and range. Set the contract's min_entities to 3 per policy for failed_orders_after_slowdown, recovered_within_window, seconds_to_recover and attempts_per_order_after.

Editor.problem: The title says 'Your Service Didn't' recover, but no gate checks that. reproduce.sh only requires failed_after > 0. A naive run that limps back to 95% at second 90 would pass and still contradict the title. seconds_to_recover is also measured for budget only, so the two policies can't be compared on recovery.
Editor.fix: Make the naive gate require recovered_within_window[naive]=0 in every repeat. If any naive run recovers, change the title to the measured gap. Measure seconds_to_recover for both policies. When a run does not recover, record it as '>120' instead of leaving it out.

Editor.problem: The takeaway says instant retries keep inventory 'busy with work nobody is waiting for'. Nothing in the contract measures that. inventory_handled_per_second only shows throughput. It cannot show whether that work was abandoned, or whether inventory, orders' CPU or the TCP listen backlog was the bottleneck. Orders runs 400 Python threads under OTel instrumentation on a 100m CPU request, on the same node as inventory and the collector agent. A busy node could produce the storm on its own.
Editor.fix: In the inventory log, record queue wait per request and whether the client had already disconnected when the response was written. Add measurements for inventory_abandoned_work_after (count and share), per-second queue depth, and per-second CPU for the orders and inventory pods and the app node. Print the effective server config (worker count, request_queue_size/listen backlog, somaxconn) in start_run so readers can see the cause.

Editor.problem: BRIEF.tradeoffs promise the post 'shows how many' orders fail without a retry while the budget is spent, and that backoff adds latency. Neither is in the measurements list, so the honest trade-off section would rest on no data.
Editor.fix: Have orders log each retry it skips because the budget is spent, plus end-to-end order latency. Add measurements for retries_denied_by_budget_after (count, budget) and p50/p99 order latency for successful orders in the 120 s window (naive, budget).

Editor.problem: The takeaway says 'Splunk APM shows the difference on the service map and request charts'. fix.sh only pulls two service.request.count totals after a fixed 'sleep 45'. No service map or chart is captured, nothing checks that Splunk's counts match the lab's own logs, and 45 s may not be long enough for the data to arrive, which could make the counts read low.
Editor.fix: Poll apm_count until two reads in a row agree, up to a cap, instead of sleeping. Add a measurement splunk_vs_log_agreement_pct comparing Splunk's inventory and orders request counts with the logs for the same window, with an accept tolerance such as within 10%. Also export the per-10 s request/error series for inventory and orders, and a service-map capture for each run's window, so the article can show what readers will see in Splunk APM.

Editor.problem: The 'one change' (RETRY_MODE=budget) actually bundles three changes: exponential backoff, full jitter and a 10% retry budget. The brief's rule is to change one setting per run so each fix can be credited, and this plan can't tell the reader which part brought the recovery.
Editor.fix: Add a third mode, backoff with full jitter and no budget, run with the same repeats. Or change the takeaway and title to credit the combination only, and drop any claim about which part matters.
